fields.title: Polden: Company Onboarding Doubles, Lunch Orders Remain Flat
fields.summary: Acquisition doubled, but revenue is flat. Marketing wants to double the budget again. Decide what to do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do next quarter and why?
fields.brief/role: You are in charge of marketing at Polden.
fields.brief/company: Polden is a fictional office lunch delivery service. The company signs the contract, employees order, and the company pays per order placed.
fields.brief/context: Over six months, onboarded companies grew from 120 to 240. Revenue grew by 9%. Marketing presents a report showing sign-up growth and asks to double the budget again. An HR conference takes place in a month. Last week, the main competitor cut lunch prices by 15%.
fields.brief/objective: Determine where to invest next quarter to drive revenue rather than just logo count.
fields.brief/constraints: You and one marketer. Budget allows for one major move: doubling acquisition, an event booth, or working with existing accounts.
fields.brief/task: Decide what to do next quarter and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: When one buyer pays and another user consumes
fields.learnTakeaway/body: In B2B2C products where a company signs the contract but employees get the value, it's easy to confuse your audience. Corporate onboarding is permission to communicate, not the end result; internal adoption requires a separate messaging strategy. To find where drop-off happens, look at two numbers: if repeat usage is high but activation is low, fix onboarding, not the product core.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Onboarded companies: 120 → 240 over six months.
Revenue: +9%.

By company: share of offices where at least half of employees ordered in the first month dropped from 54% to 31%.
The average office places 0.8 orders per employee per week; offices onboarded six months ago average 2.3.

Employee funnel within an onboarded office: learned about service 100% (HR email) → opened app 44% → placed first order 19% → ordered a second time 61%.

Analyst: "Nearly two-thirds place a second order. The issue isn't food quality or price—only one in five ever places their first order."
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Eight interviews: four office managers, four employees.

Office managers sign up to solve the "how to feed staff" task and judge the service by the lack of complaints. None mentioned price.

Employees: "HR sent an email, I skimmed it." Three out of four didn't realize the company pays for the meal, mistaking it for corporate discounts. One noted: "I thought it was like corporate gym perks—nice to have, but unclear if I need it."

Not a single employee cited price as an obstacle.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The competitor reduced lunch prices by 15% and announced it via an industry newsletter. They have 900 onboarded companies.

In comment sections, office managers ask mostly about on-time delivery, not price.

HR conference is in a month. Last year Polden attended to "spread awareness": collected 45 leads, onboarded 2 companies—both averaging just one office order per month.

You have a 40-person office client where, three months post-onboarding, employees average 2.6 orders per week. Baseline metrics exist: they used to eat across the street with a 52-minute lunch break, now down to 28 minutes. They agreed to be featured as a public case study.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Office onboarding finishes with HR emailing employees using a template provided by you.

Template text: "The company has partnered with Polden lunch delivery. Register in the app via this link. Meals available from 12 restaurants, menu updates daily at 9:00 AM."

Email open rate is 38%, click rate is 11%.

App update notes go out to employees biweekly: "Updated checkout UI, bug fixes, added new restaurants."

The marketer asks what to write instead.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix employee activation instead of company acquisition
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Tailor messaging separately for office managers and employees, clarify that the company pays, support with data-backed case studies, and track offices where over half of employees order in month one.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The employee email template is rewritten: "Lunch is paid for by the company. Order before 11:00 AM for delivery by your break. Another office reduced lunch breaks from 52 to 28 minutes."
Email click rates rise from 11% to 29%, first orders jump from 19% to 34%. Repeat order retention holds steady at 61%.
Release notes shift focus to user value and drop to a monthly cadence.
Over the quarter, company sign-ups reach only 265, but revenue leaps by 34% as older accounts order at the rate of seasoned accounts.
Trade-off: marketing acquisition reports look modest, and you skipped the HR conference.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Acquisition is working. Give marketing more budget to reach 500 onboarded companies in a quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
By quarter-end, 470 companies are onboarded. Reports look stellar.
Revenue increases by 12%. The share of offices where at least half of employees order drops from 31% to 24%, as new offices receive the same generic email template.
Operational overhead balloons with contract onboarding, yielding minimal order volume.
A quarter later, you face the exact same issue at a larger scale.
Trade-off: you scaled what was working while scaling the broken activation step alongside it.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The competitor cut prices by 15%, so accounts will compare options. Match the discount to prevent churn.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
You cut prices by 12%. Account churn remains flat—though it was never an issue: two accounts left this quarter, same as the last.
Revenue drops 7% on identical order volume.
Post-mortem reveals what survey data showed all along: neither employees nor office managers cited price as a problem, and competitor feedback focused entirely on delivery reliability.
Trade-off: you reacted to industry noise without assessing its strategic impact, sacrificing profit margin.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Attend HR conference with a case study
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Decision-makers gather there. Present the case study on reduced lunch breaks to acquire new company accounts.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The case study turns out strong: 2.6 orders per employee, a break of 28 minutes instead of 52, a before-measurement, and consent to be named.
6 companies sign up compared to two last year — a case study with a number works better than a story about the service.
But all six receive the same email template, and a month later only 18–20% of employees in them place orders. Revenue barely moves.
Trade-off: you improved the most expensive channel and didn't touch the step where four people out of five are lost.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Conversion is viewed as a single aggregate metric without funnel stage or source breakdowns
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Acquisition growth is evaluated independently of downstream retention and usage
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Messaging focuses on product features without highlighting concrete user benefits or proof
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The same message is recycled across all stages of user awareness and funnel steps
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Market news is treated as actionable signal without evaluating if it alters strategy
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Event participation lacks a verifiable objective or measurable success criteria
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Release notes report internal engineering outputs rather than user value changes
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: Case study is presented without quantitative proof or context, offering no real evidence
